subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO AGENDA FOR DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO AGENDA FOR DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I ask the right hon. Prime Minister about the agenda for the federal-provincial conference which is to be held

early in the new year. In view of the fact that the letter of invitation which the Prime Minister sent to the premiers, dated August 15, mentions only a proposed bill of rights, could I ask the Prime Minister whether it is the intention of the government to widen the agenda for the conference so as to deal with some of the problems which were posed by the confederation of tomorrow conference and which still have to be resolved?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. B. Pearson (Prime Minister):
subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO AGENDA FOR DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE
speechtext: In the invitation to the conference it was suggested to the premiers that while we had called this conference to discuss a very important constitutional matter, a federal bill of rights, we would welcome any suggestions the provincial governments might make as to the widening of the agenda, because we did not wish to restrict it in any way. I may have one suggestion to make with regard to that matter this afternoon when I make my statement on the B and B commission report.

subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO AGENDA FOR DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE
speechtext: A supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. May I ask the Prime Minister whether it will be possible to have a copy of the agenda made public prior to the conference; and is it the intention of the government to present a statement setting forth the particular parts of the constitution which may have to be revised in order to give the federal government the necessary powers to develop a viable and expanding economy? I would also ask whether such a statement will be made prior to the conference.

subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO AGENDA FOR DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, so far as making public the agenda before the conference meets is concerned, I have no objection whatever to that. I would wish to wait, of course, until we get the views of the provinces as to what they would like included in the agenda. I hope this will be done in ample time for the agenda to be made public before the conference meets. As far as the other part of the question is concerned, I should like to look into the possibility of a statement being made along the lines suggested before the conference opens.

subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO AGENDA FOR DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE
speechtext: Has there been a decision, or is the question still under discussion, as to the extent to which the conference will be held in public?

subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO AGENDA FOR DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE
speechtext:
No decision has been taken on that point; that will have to be decided by those participating in the conference. I would be very glad to take that up well in advance
December 5, 1967

of the meeting so the greatest possible publicity can be given to this meeting.

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert L. Stanfield (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO AGENDA FOR DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE
speechtext: A supplementary question to the Prime Minister relating to the constitutional conference. Does the Prime Minister have in mind seeking the opinion of the house prior to the conference on any of the questions to be discussed with the provinces?

subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO AGENDA FOR DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE
speechtext:
That would depend, of
course, to some extent on the date which is agreed upon. It is conceivable, though I hope it will not happen, that the house may not be sitting on that date. I have suggested to the provinces that the conference might meet in the first week of February; I shall be glad, if parliament is sitting before that-and it may well be sitting before that-to consider the possibility of a day being set aside in the Commons to consider the matters to come before the conference.

subtopic: PAYMENT OF SUBSISTENCE ALLOWANCES DURING CHRISTMAS HOLIDAYS

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Mr. J. E. Pascoe (Moose Jaw-Lake Centre):
subtopic: PAYMENT OF SUBSISTENCE ALLOWANCES DURING CHRISTMAS HOLIDAYS
speechtext: I have a question for the Minister of Manpower and Immigration. Is it the policy of his department to cut off for two weeks at Christmas and the New Year the living allowance paid to those taking adult occupational training courses under government sponsorship at technical institutes across Canada?

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean Marchand (Minister of Manpower and Immigration):
subtopic: PAYMENT OF SUBSISTENCE ALLOWANCES DURING CHRISTMAS HOLIDAYS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think I have already explained the policy of the government to the house.
Those who are assigned to these training courses are, according to our way of thinking, simple workers: they are not people who are going back to school, but workers. They play an essential role in our economy and must therefore be treated like other workers: They must have the same holidays and receive allowances which are in a way comparable to those of other workers.
If courses are given during the holidays, these workers will receive allowances, just like those who work in a factory. If there are no courses, naturally, they will not receive allowances, but they may be eligible for unemployment insurance.

December 5, 1967
Inquiries of the Ministry

subtopic: PAYMENT OF SUBSISTENCE ALLOWANCES DURING CHRISTMAS HOLIDAYS
speechtext:

view of the fact that most of the students taking these courses were formerly unemployed, and since many of them are married and have families, would the government not reconsider its policy so the living allowance could be continued? subtopic: PAYMENT OF SUBSISTENCE ALLOWANCES DURING CHRISTMAS HOLIDAYS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I think it is incumbent on the provinces to organize courses so that the situation described by my hon. friend does not take place.

subtopic: PAYMENT OF SUBSISTENCE ALLOWANCES DURING CHRISTMAS HOLIDAYS

speechtext:
On the orders of the day:
Hon. Georg* Hees (Northumberland):	I
should like to address a question to the Min-
ister of Finance. In view of a statement by the Economic Council of Canada that businessmen are not planning sufficient capital investment during the next five years to keep the economy growing to its full potential, is it the intention of the government to introduce measures in the near future to induce the necessary additional capital investment?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO STEPS TO INCREASE CAPITAL INVESTMENT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the chairman of the Economic Council of Canada gave similar information to the finance ministers' meeting recently. subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO STEPS TO INCREASE CAPITAL INVESTMENT
speechtext: Will the minister assure the house that he will report back to the house when he has had an opportunity of carrying on these further discussions, and then outline the intentions of the government in this regard?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO STEPS TO INCREASE CAPITAL INVESTMENT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the government's policies in all these respects are revealed from time to time. I do not believe it would be appropriate for me to make a special report to the house on this matter.

subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO STEPS TO INCREASE CAPITAL INVESTMENT
speechtext: I should like to direct this question also to the Minister of Finance. speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO STEPS TO INCREASE CAPITAL INVESTMENT
speechtext: No, I have not seen this particular prediction. I have seen many on the other side, and I am sure the views of economists on the outlook, as usual, are quite confused.

subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO STEPS TO INCREASE CAPITAL INVESTMENT
speechtext: In view of the minister's reply, will the minister now admit he is an economist?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO STEPS TO INCREASE CAPITAL INVESTMENT
speechtext: No, I would never admit that.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, before this legislation passes I would like to speak about the effects, if any, which the over-all capital expenditures of the C.N.R. are having on freight rates and about the new environment which we are told is developing for the transport industry generally.
I know that one of the dearest dreams of the former president of the C.N.R. was to secure a reorganization of the company's debt, which he told us many times was one of the biggest stumbling blocks to the C.N.R. ever operating in the black. Under the terms of this bill, parliament is being asked to confirm moneys already being spent by the C.N.R., and I would point out that the amount involved is larger than that provided by any similar bill placed before parliament in past years. Since the early 1950's the C.N.R. has engaged in massive capital expenditures, but despite the increase in productivity which they brought about, accompanied by a decrease in the cost of moving freight per ton mile, the position of the company has not really improved.
One may well ask, what is the effect of these capital expenditures on freight costs and why we are being asked to ratify or approve expenditures already made? According to the bill $13 million has been or will be spent before the end of the year on the building of branch lines. Yet only a year or so ago this house spent a long time studying the new transportation act which was designed to create a new environment for the transport industry. One of the purposes of that act was to allow the railroads to abandon branch lines. But under the terms of this bill parliament is now being asked to provide money for the construction of branch lines, particularly in western Canada.
Uneconomic branch lines have a tendency to increase freight rates. Under the terms of this bill the C.N.R. is being provided with money to construct in one location in western Canada a 17-mile branch line which is to run within two or three miles of an existing C.P.R. main line. This just does not add up.
What about the new environment which the transportation commission is supposed to encourage? What have been the results? This is the question which is being asked by many people, particularly those in western Canada. Last October there was a 10 per cent increase in freight rates across the board covering all rates that were not frozen by the previous government. The only result of that increase
December 5, 1967	COMMONS
in freight rates has been that the traffic moved by the C.N.R. has diminished in volume.
The principle involved in this bill, which is to ratify expenditures already made, is putting the cart before the horse. If parliament is to have any authority at all there should be some means of ratifying a capital expenditure bill for the C.N.R. before the C.N.R. has actually undertaken expenditures. Last year parliament spent a long time debating the rationalization of the abandonment of branch lines; yet now it is asked to authorize $13 million to build branch lines. Is this good, efficient government?
The capital expenditure to be authorized by this bill is the largest ever authorized by parliament for the C.N.R. in the past 15 years, yet there is no real reduction in the cost of moving goods by the C.N.R. We realize it takes money to automate and establish an up to date transportation system, but the customer should be getting a return on that money. He should be paying less to move goods by the C.N.R., but the direct opposite has happened. There has been a huge increase in freight rates since the ceiling on them was removed. Freight rates in the mari-times have also increased and many firms are being forced out of business.
Despite all the talk about a new environment for transport, the old theory holds true that the railway freight rate is the minimum rate charged by most forms of transport. It is the rate which the trucking industry applies. In effect it is the floor price for the transportation of goods, and competition does not have any real effect. This is particularly the case in western Canada where the only means of competition is by highway. Yet methods could be found to create a greater competitive spirit in the transportation field.

So there is no real competition in the transportation industry, particularly in respect of long haul traffic. This is the situation in western Canada and, as we have heard, it is also the situation in the maritimes.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to table copies in English and in French of the first report, volume 1 as it is called, and a very important report of the royal commission on bilingualism and biculturalism. The recommendations in this report, which are of far reaching significance, deal with the status of the two official languages of Canada. The report was made available to the government late last week and has already been the subject of consideration by the cabinet. The government has established machinery which will ensure
Bilingualism and Biculturalism that all the recommendations of the report are given serious and urgent appraisal so that the government may be in a position to make its views known without undue delay and to take whatever action is required.
I wish to state immediately, Mr. Speaker, what I have already said before more than once, that the government fully endorses the principle of French speaking and English speaking linguistic and cultural equality that forms the core of and is so clearly defined in this report. The report includes 14 recommendations, six of which deal with matters that are primarily for consideration by provincial governments; three would involve joint consideration and, if agreed, joint action by the federal and provincial governments; two are recommendations for constitutional amendment, while the remaining three lie within the jurisdiction of the federal government.
It is the intention of the government to deal as quickly as possible with those matters in this report which fall within its constitutional jurisdiction. The recommendations, of course, are also of the utmost importance and interest to provincial governments and copies of the report are being made available to each of those governments. I am suggesting also to the provinces that a discussion of matters in the report should be included in the agenda of the forthcoming federal-provincial constitutional conference which is to be held early next year. I hope that discussion with and consideration by the provinces will lead to agreement concerning all matters that involve their participation or require a constitutional amendment.
Since the royal commission was appointed in 1963 the matters which were outlined in its terms of reference have been under increasing examination within the country, and this has led to a greater understanding of the problems involved and of the necessity to work co-operatively to find solutions for them, as I am sure we can do. Since the commission was established the federal government has taken a number of important steps, some of which have a bearing on the recommendations in this particular report. For some time, for instance, policies have been in operation to promote bilingualism in the public service of Canada. The federal government has also initiated, in co-operation with the governments of Ontario and Quebec, a study of the necessary steps which should be taken co-operatively among the three governments and in consultation with the
December 5. 1967

Bilingualism and Biculturalism municipalities concerned to develop a truly national capital area extending on both sides of the Ottawa river. The government will be announcing in due course other steps which relate to the recommendations in this report.
In the meantime, Mr. Speaker, I can assure the house that the report and its implications are being studied most carefully, as its importance demands. I am sure that all provincial governments will want to give this report the same careful attention. I should like to thank the members of the commission, Mr. Speaker, for this further evidence of the responsible and constructive approach they are making to the various and important matters entrusted to them for examination and report. They are exploring and clarifying problems, fundamental problems, of Canadian unity, diversity and federalism in the circumstances of today. By doing so they are giving invaluable assistance to all those who are searching in a sincere and positive way for solutions to these problems. Such solutions, based on unity in diversity, of equality and partnership, are essential to Canadian development, indeed to Canadian survival. They must, they will be found, Mr. Speaker, so that Canada can live and grow and provide a good life for all its people.

The commission's terms of reference dealt only with the matter of bilingualism and biculturalism, but it seems to me that the conference to be held early in the new year must begin to tackle the wider problem of Canadian confederation. Since the commission will not be dealing with that subject there is no need to wait for further reports before proceeding with a discussion between federal and provincial governments of the matter.

It is sometimes said that what the French speaking Canadians want is to feel at home in every part of Canada. I think they want even more than that. Mr. Speaker, we have listened with interest to the statement made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) this afternoon on the tabling of the first report of the royal commission on bilingualism and biculturalism.
At the time the commission was appointed many questions were asked. For instance, many Canadians wondered whether the appointment of such a commission would contribute to unity and harmony in Canada or whether it would be an additional divisive factor. Others wondered whether there would be an impartial inquiry into the questions within the commission's terms of reference or whether it had been appointed to do a selling job on a course to which the government was
5070	COMMONS
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion already committed. In addition, the question was asked whether there was any real justification for the expenditure of the vast sums of public money which, even in the very earliest stages, it was evident would be required. Another question raised at the time of the appointment of the commission was whether any consideration would be given to the one third of the population of Canada who are neither English nor French speaking.
I suggest these are the questions that will be uppermost in the minds of Canadians in general when they have the opportunity to consider the report that has just been tabled. Of course it is impossible to grasp the full significance of the report without a very careful analysis of it. Indications are that its recommendations will be very far reaching, but on other occasions we will have opportunities to deal with them in some detail.
I agree with the suggestion that it will be necessary for us to receive all the reports of the commission before we are able to understand in a really broad sense the objectives which the commission has in mind. I trust that the remaining reports will not be too long delayed.
The implementation of many of the recommendations will be dependent not so much on constitutional change but on the co-operation of the provinces concerned. The Prime Minister has indicated that there are a number of recommendations, I believe six, which come almost entirely within provincial jurisdiction and others come under shared jurisdiction. I suggest that any attempt to infringe on provincial prerogatives in this connection or to exercise undue pressure or coercion could have very serious and unfortunate results. May I also suggest that any changes in the linguistic or cultural nature of Canada which may result from the implementation of any or all of these recommendations must not be used to promote undesirable changes in our political and constitutional structure.
I am sure the report will be studied very carefully in every part of Canada. We trust that our country will be able to move forward unitedly to achieve the destiny which is desirable and possible for us.

subtopic: CABRI PIPE LINES LTD.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I am interested in the number of pipe line bills that we have been getting, particularly in the wording detailing their purposes. I think it is safe to say that we are unduly cautious about passing pipe line bills for the simple reason that the companies involved are never clear as to what they want and what they are going to do. This is a bill that falls into that category.
I do not know whether it is wise for us to have a number of small international or interprovincial companies constructing pipe lines over short distances such as in the present case. The length of the pipe line is to be 20 miles, but it will cross an interprovincial boundary. From reading the questions asked during the committee proceedings on this bill I understand that incorporation of this pipe line company could have taken place in several other ways. The pipe line is to run from a particular well to a delivery point in the Lloydminster area where I assume the product it carries will be used. I also assume that initially the product will be gas which will be used in the immediate area. If this were so, there would certainly be no opposition to the incorporation of this company. It would be a supplier moving its product to a restricted market in a given area. But that is not what the bill seeks.
[DOT] (6:10 p.m.)
I have read the remarks of the sponsor. I have read the remarks made by the parliamentary agent and by the counsel for this
December 5, 1967

corporation. This is not what they say the bill is for. I should like to quote some of the evidence which was given before the committee on transport and communications on November 28, 1967. This evidence is not necessarily the same as the evidence given before the committee of the other place in respect of this company. The hon. member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace said:
Sir, you said that you were asking for more powers-
More powers than were outlined in the simple explanation originally given.
-because it would be an interprovincial pipe line. I notice in clause 6 that you are also asking for powers for international pipe lines.
This was the answer:

Yes; the international feature has been included because it is very difficult to predict where the markets of the future will be and consequently it has been a standard custom in the case of pipe line companies to loop them both interprovincially and/or internationally.
If this is really what this company wants to do, it should have said so in the first place. It is quite true that it may have a number of wells and may expand, but it is my contention that if it wants to do that it should be willing to come back and obtain an amendment. The company told the committee that what is involved is a simple pipe line 20 miles in length. I suppose the situation is like that when a person is asking for an increase in salary. He asks for ten times as much as he expects to get. In this case the company is asking for an international charter to transport gas 20 miles. I think this raises a problem. I know there are many lawyers in this house. They may think that the other place has hit on the best format for bringing these companies into existence. They may be right, but I believe it is an imposition on hon. members when someone comes before parliament asking for this type of incorporation and then says that what is involved is a 20 mile four inch gas line.
There are not very many communities in Ontario which do not have a line with a capacity four or five times that size. This is a four inch gas pipe line and yet they are asking for authority for a facility to handle a refinery or an international transportation line. The potential they are asking for is similar to the capitalization. They are asking for $4 million. I do not think it will be necessary to raise $4 million.
They really have not told us who they are. The lawyer told us that he is a Canadian who acts for a number of gas companies. I suppose a lawyer could also say that he is connected with a dozen murderers, but this does not necessarily connect him with the crimes. This is the only person who appeared to speak for the company. A number of companies were mentioned. It was stated that the president of Cabri is Mr. Stanley Milner of Edmonton, who is president of Chieftain Development Company Limited, and that he is very active in the west and prominent in other related companies including Blue Crown Petroleums Limited and Lloydminster Gas Company Limited.
Although it was not mentioned, I presume that one of these companies is doing the drilling and has the well. They indicate that one company will be used for the purpose of supplying the gas. I presume that this will be Lloydminster Gas Company Limited. It seems to me that we are getting all cluttered up with these little companies. Here we have a person who incorporates a company to do a certain type of business such as delivering gas. He sets up at least two companies and then a third. One will do the drilling, another will handle the distribution and the third, an international and interprovincial company with federal incorporation, will handle the transportation. He asks for a capitalization of $4 million. While this company probably is a bona fide company and is probably making a bona fide request, I believe that if members will look at the evidence that was given they will find that the company is asking for things which it probably does not want. I suggest that if this is the situation it should not have this type of incorporation.

December 5, 1967
Private Bills
I agree that in the past we have caused many of these companies problems and they may think that if they can get the kitchen sink they will be better off, because if they failed to ask for it they would have to come back again. After reading the answers of this lawyer 1 would suggest that he did not tell us all he knows. It was only after members of the committee questioned him that he provided the interesting information on these matters.
[DOT] (6:20 p.m.)
It may be that the company is asking for authority to construct 20 miles of four inch pipeline to look after an expansion in business in the future, but this does not mean the company will go into the business of refining. I do not know how many refineries there are in western Canada but I understand the number is limited because of cost. Why should a small gas company with one well spend half a billion dollars to build a refinery and associated facilities in order to make this an economically feasible development? I do not think this company needs one red cent to incorporate. I imagine Mr. Milner will just dig into another company pocket to provide the money for this operation.
I do not understand why these people seeking federal incorporation do not go for the whole shooting match and then do everything under the one company name. During the committee meetings one hon. member asked several questions of Mr. Cressey. He said:
First of all, Mr. Cressey, I am rather intrigued by the name. Why did you call it Cabri Pipe Lines? The only Cabri I know is quite a long distance away from Lloydminster, and it happens to be in my constituency.
I do not know where the hon. member's constituency is, but Mr. Cressey in answer said:
Mr. McKiram pointed out that he was not sure about my qualifications in other fields, but I have been involved in pipe line business for some years, and I was engaged in the pipe line facilities constructed through Cabri. There is always the problem of seizing upon a name that has not been used in some other context by some other company in Canada, and I thought I was fairly safe in picking the very small community of Cabri.
I am in agreement with that statement. Every year we pass five or six pipe line bills which involve names conflicting with the names of other companies. In this case the company adopted the name of a very small community. It is interesting to note that the solicitor for the company has been connected with other pipe lines for some period of time.

He was apparently connected with the construction of a line going through that area. It is probably safe to say that Mr. Cressey has not informed the committee of all his connections with pipe line companies.
Why should parliament be asked to incorporate a company such as Bell Telephone in order to enable it to put a satellite on the moon when it is interested really in putting a satellite on Mars? Cabri does not really want authority to operate an international pipe line company but it has been the practice of lawyers to draft these bills in this manner, asking for everything, because the cost is exactly the same and the company receives international export rights. They might just as well ask for authority to build all the other facilities involved such as townsites, airports, housing, stores, roads and communication lines.
I have no doubt that this is a bona fide company, particularly in view of its limited size. However, when the company asks for something it does not need or want, then I think for the sake of good housekeeping if for no other reason we should consider their requests very carefully to determine how much is necessary. These companies continue to come to parliament for incorporation. I suggest that within a year or two they will stop coming here because they will have learned by then that we do not intend to accede to their requests. Maybe they will come then with properly drafted bills. I am not sure this company will come back again for incorporation, but if it does it will have to come with a bill that has been cleaned up, containing requests for authorization to construct the things it needs. It seems foolish for these people to come before a committee and say they do not actually intend to do that for which they seek authorization. This is like someone suggesting he hopes to swim the Atlantic ocean but knows he will never try. These requests of the company should be relevant to the services they intend to provide. They should not try to fool people by asking for authorization to carry on certain services they do not intend to provide.
For these reasons I suggest to Mr. Cressey and his parliamentary agent that if they intend to serve in a responsible way they will make known their exact plans after incorporation. They should stop misleading people by cluttering the records. This practice will not be allowed to continue indefinitely and perhaps this word to the wise will be sufficient.

Mr. Chairman, I listened with a great deal of interest to the remarks of the hon. member for Timiskaming regarding the proposal to incorporate Cabri Pipe Lines Limited. As I did so I recalled my experience not long after I became a member of this house. I was a member of the old railways, canals and telegraph lines committee which had a bill before it seeking authorization to permit one of our national railway systems to construct a small branch line. This line did not involve a distance of more than 20 miles. I was puzzled that the company had to come before parliament to obtain a special act in order to construct a short spur line from an existing line to another point.
The development officers of the railway company spelled out in great detail the economics involved in the construction of that spur line, the cost of construction and the nature of the freight they intended to carry. I became even more puzzled and began to look into the matter. I then realized that parliament had created a situation which forced these companies to come before parliament with bills of this kind. I discovered that this practice arose out of the history of the development of transportation facilities. It stemmed from the fact that from past experience we learned there have been unregulated and unwise expansions of railway lines to the extent that at one point in our history this development came near to bankrupting the nation.
[DOT] (6:30 p.m.)
Then I began to realize why a previous parliament had placed this kind of restriction upon the national railway companies. I mention this to emphasize why in my opinion it is absurd that in this day and age parliament should be satisfied to allow a company concerned with another mode of transportation to come before it with this vague, general, ombinus sort of bill. I refer to companies with backgrounds such as were pointed out by the hon. member for Timiskaming. When this bill is boiled down, it is simply concerned with a company applying to construct approximately 20 miles of 4-inch pipe line.
The question I ask the committee is, why do we allow this absurd situation to continue, wherein we are willing to allow companies to come before us with this sort of bill, although in the past parliament saw fit to place restrictions upon the freedom and ability of railway companies which developed national transportation systems? A previous parliament required such railway companies to

come before parliament with specific proposals to construct a line from point A to point B. As the hon. member for Timiskaming said, those of us from this quarter of the house who are speaking on this bill, as we have spoken on others, are not in any way objecting to the fact that a pipe fine should be constructed from point A to point B in order to carry a certain petroleum product. We object to the fact that on one hand we require a railway company to come before parliament with a specific proposal in a bill to construct a specific piece of line, and on the other we allow certain interests to come before us with a vague, generalized proposition which, as the hon. member for Timiskaming said, might allow them to build a pipe line to the moon.
I have read the evidence given to the committee and recognize the desire to construct this piece of pipe line in a location which crosses provincial boundaries, and therefore federal action is necessary. We have no quarrel with the fact that because of this particular geographic circumstance parliament should be asked to deal with it. What we are concerned about, as the hon. member for Timiskaming said, is the process of companies being incorporated ad nauseam, with blanket powers in their charters of incorporation, to build national and international pipe lines. We are concerned that this practice be not continued because in my view it is making a mockery of parliament. I think the point of the hon. member for Timiskaming was well taken, that the legal fraternity which had been advising these companies should smarten up and suggest to them it is about time they got down to brass tacks.
Some fairly searching questions were asked in the committee. This I welcome. I noticed that the hon. member for Kootenay East raised the question as to whether this pipe line would be a common carrier. The answer given by the spokesman for the applicant was that it would be. That may or may not be necessary and desirable in this particular circumstance. If it is a matter of carrying the products of more than one company to be distributed to more than one consumer, 1 suppose it is necessary and desirable that it should be a common carrier. But on the face of it, it seems rather strange that a picayune proposal of this kind should require that the company set itself up as a common carrier.
I find this feature of the bill rather puzzling, perhaps because in that part of the

December 5, 1967

country in which I live various concerns involved in the production of some of our products build transportation facilities. It is true that these are not pipe lines, but hundreds and indeed thousands of miles of roads are built for the purpose of transporting their commodities. As long as those roads are being used exclusively for the transportation of the product of one company, they remain in effect, private roads.
If one examines this process, and were able to look into all the ramifications of the different companies in which the people applying in this instance seem to be involved, perhaps the real necessity for the proposed pipe line being constructed in this form arises from the fact that with various corporate structures it will be possible for the profit picture of the shareholders to be improved somewhat, artificially, and at the same time perhaps to be concealed. There is an old saying about dividing and ruling with which we are all familiar.
It seems that in this process which we are allowing to continue, namely the development of facilities for transporting commodities by pipe line, we are creating a corporate maze in which the Canadian people are becoming increasingly snared and which is becoming so complicated that any ordinary citizen, and citizens generally and collectively, may find a great deal of difficulty finding their way out.
I know it is always said in these committee hearings that the bill is in the ordinary form. The point I am trying to make is that as far as I am concerned this bill is in an extraordinarily unnecessary form. This is the point that perhaps should be primarily emphasized in relation to it. It may be that the form of this bill is even more extraordinary and unnecessary than has been the case with bills of a similar nature with which we have been called upon to deal.
Like the hon. member for Timiskaming, I found rather intriguing the little bit of evidence that had to do with how this name was picked. I was interested to learn from the hon. member for Kindersley, who apparently is more familiar with the community of Cabri than most members of the house, that it is a very nice community. I am not at all sure, however, that the people of this community should take it as a compliment that this pipe company should, in a sense, have pre-empted their name, just because so many of these companies are being formed that it is becoming increasingly difficult to pick suitable names.
[Mr. Barnett.l
[DOT] (6:40 p.m.)
In my view, granting these broad powers to a multiplicity of concerns can only lead ultimately to confusion and the strangulation of any attempt to produce an effective system of transportation of the commodities by pipe line across this country. I notice for example that this company is seeking the right to transport solids. Well, there is another bill somewhere in the parliamentary hopper designed to enable a company to move into the solids pipe line field, which is likely to become an increasingly important method of transportation. Even though these matters are subject to the jurisdiction of the Canadian Transport Commission or the National Energy Board, if we continue to grant such powers as these to all who apply for them we shall be loading down those public bodies with an increasingly complicated task when they endeavour, as they will have to do one day in the future, to rationalize the hodgepodge which we in parliament have created.
These are some of the considerations which should be of concern to the committee in relation to these applications. The fact that the application before us involves such a relatively minor construction project makes it all the more necessary to emphasize the ridiculousness of the situation while we are dealing with this particular bill. If the committee passes the clause now under consideration, I believe it should give careful study to some of the following clauses. Hon. members might even consider whether we ought not to eliminate some of the more ridiculous aspects of the bill as it now stands. Having done so, we might be in a better position to judge whether the bill as a whole should receive approval.

The general subject opened up by my hon. friend from Timiskaming and dealt with by my hon. friend from Comox-Alberni is an intriguing one. The scope of the powers sought by this bill certainly does not correspond with the reality of the situation.
With respect, and without wishing to misinterpret in any way what the hon. member for Provencher said on second reading, this disparity was certainly not in the mind of that hon. member, either. For this reason I believe it is an extremely valid point to say that many of these unnecessary and unwanted powers should at an appropriate stage, perhaps when we get to clause 6, be removed from the bill in order that the company may obtain simply the authority to do what it desires to do immediately with respect to
December 5, 1967

transporting gas from one province to another, a distance of 20 miles or so.
When I say it is my impression that the hon. member for Provencher undoubtedly has had the same sort of understanding as did the officers of the company, namely that the activities contemplated would be somewhat limited, I am bearing in mind the remarks he made on November 9 when the bill was given second reading. Those observations, I believe, substantiate my impression.
Listening to the words of the hon. member at that time led me to believe that this company was seeking incorporation in order to perform only the minor function or service described. As a consequence I pursued the matter no further; I did not even look into the bill in any detail. It was not until my hon. friend from Timiskaming dealt with the subject that I began to realize the enormity of the proposition now before us.
Perhaps I can quote from page 4102 of Hansard in connection with what the hon. member had to say on second reading. I have no desire to quote him out of context or to misrepresent him; only to quote those parts which gave me and other members the impression that the bill was a simple one, seeking authority to build a pipe line for a distance of some 20 miles. Subsequent discussions in the standing committee showed, of course, that this is really not the case. The hon. member for Provencher said:
What the bill proposes is a storage facility in connection with a gas distribution company. It will be located across the Alberta-Saskatchewan border. The distribution company is seeking permission to build a pipe line connecting producing wells with a dry hole located some distance from the Alberta border in Saskatchewan where gas will be stored.
This is a simple, uncomplicated declaration of what the company proposes to do. There is no reference to running a television network or operating aircraft or international pipe lines or interprovincial pipe lines. It is a simple business of transporting gas from one province to another. The hon. member went on to point out that the demand for natural gas is higher in the winter than in the summer, but that natural gas can be recovered at a much greater rate in the summer when demand is low. The object, then, is to produce a balanced supply of gas for the area receiving it.

The hon. member said the sponsors of the bill were all Canadians, and then he went on to state this:
The passage of the bill will allow this company to put its operations on a more economical and efficient basis.
The operations referred to are presumably those connected with the distribution of gas.
A federal incorporation is necessary because the construction of this line will be interprovincial, running between the provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan.
Almost as an afterthought, or as an aside, the hon. member went on to say:
The powers requested are necessary in the event that further lines are required. If this is the case, the company must again apply to the National Energy Board-
[DOT] (6:50 p.m.)
The point is that the hon. member's explanation of the purpose of the bill was that it had to do with the building of a pipe line to transport natural gas from one province to another, and store it so that the operation of the company would be on a more economical basis. In this way, the natural gas would be available at an even level during both summer and winter. The reference to the powers requested at that juncture was to the effect they are requested in the event further lines were required. This was thrown in as an incidental part of the commentary by the hon. member for Provencher.
As I said at the outset, I do not mean to misrepresent what he said, but this was the impression I got from listening to his remarks on second reading, and that impression is substantiated from reading those remarks into the record. The impression was that the sole purpose of the company was to obtain this authority to build a pipe line across an international boundary, and that all the other matters really were not too important. The international aspect, the possibility of the company operating aircraft, operating aerodromes and microwave systems, were rather remote.
As the hon. member for Timiskaming said to me a minute ago in relation to this microwave system, the distance is only 20 miles and if a strong wind were blowing in the right direction you could holler to one another. You would not need any microwave system installed for that purpose. However, these are some of the powers sought by this particular company.
I have no great desire to delay unnecessarily the passage of the bill. As has been

December 5, 1967
Private Bills
explained to me privately, there is some urgency to give the bill passage so the company can carry out its activities and proceed to make application to the National Energy Board. However, I do believe there is something here that is of greater consequence and which should put us in the position of having a further look at the bill to ascertain whether or not, in the interim, the officers of the company might not be able to accept some alteration in the powers sought. I am referring to the powers which cover such things as movement across international borders, as well as the transportation of solids, which will be dealt with by one of my colleagues. Then, there is the matter of giving a blanket authority to operate a microwave system, television communication, radio communication and everything of a like nature, without any confinement of that power.
Usually when such power is sought in a bill like this it is limited to the purpose of the undertaking. These are the words normally used to make sure that there is no invasion into the radio, television or communications media. In recent days the members of this association met with the company in an attempt to negotiate wages and conditions, but I understand they ran into a blind alley in these negotiations. The only explanation they could get from the company officials was that any increase in pay would mean additional layoffs. I understand that these employees are working a 50 hour week and that no overtime pay is involved because of the fact that the company requested and was granted a deferment of the 40 hour work week provision of the Canada Labour Code. I do not argue about the principle of putting supervisory staff on a 40 hour week, but I do think the situation to which I have referred is a gross inconsistency.
Perhaps, Mr. Chairman, I sound quite critical of the Canadian National Railways, but I should like to make one thing clear at this point. I more or less grew up with the Canadian National Railways, having been hired at a time when the railway was run very inefficiently. It had inadequate facilities, poor track and actually was a third rate operation. He said: Well, Mr. Speaker, as I understand the arrangement I will be the one who will be getting the worst of the bargain. I will have to make the opening explanation in respect of the bill. I do not believe we will proceed very far in terms of settling the adoption of the bill. However, I think there may be something to be said for this procedure. Perhaps I can explain a little of the history behind the bill, and the spirit in which it was drafted. This in itself might give hon. members something about which to speak at a later date on second reading.
At this point I might give a little of the history of the divorce laws of this country. The western provinces of Canada are now, by and large, governed by the divorce laws of England, the laws of 1857 as later modified in 1870. In so far as Ontario is concerned, that province also, broadly speaking, is governed by the divorce laws of England of 1870 which were brought into effect by the federal legislation of 1930. In so far as the maritime provinces are concerned, they are largely governed by pre-confederation statutes and a mixture of such statutes with the common law of England ante-dating confederation. So, I believe it is fair to say that the most up to date laws governing divorce in Canada go back to 1870. Even if we consider the problem of the two provinces of Quebec and Newfoundland, which have a special status concerning divorce, they too are governed by the laws of that time.
Therefore, with laws dating back to 1870, in a society which has moved so quickly and so far in the intervening 97 years, it is not astonishing that the present divorce laws and the way in which they govern our society is highly unsatisfactory and indeed produces some very evil results. We all know, even though we may not have had a very close or direct experience with divorce, that people today who are faced with situations in which their marriages can no longer continue, are placed in a curious dilemma. In a great number of cases, either they do not get a divorce and live under common law arrangements, which are generally unsatisfactory and
Divorce Law Reform
irregular, or they go through a very hypocritical procedure of fabricating evidence and arranging proof for a divorce, which is also a hypocrisy and a sham. This is compounded by the fact that this parliament in one house, and later in the other, has over the years passed thousands of private divorce bills for at least two provinces in order to meet the situation. The people of Canada have realized that this kind of hypocrisy and sham is not satisfactory and that it is now up to this parliament to bring about a solution to this unacceptable social situation. Because of this, there has been mounting pressure from all areas for reform of divorce law. We have seen the continuing mounting pressure in many areas.
[DOT] (8:40 p.m.)
I think it would be proper at this point to underline the efforts of the many sections of the population-very laudable efforts indeed -to create the kind of public opinion in the country which permits us to tackle the problem properly.
Let me refer first to the joint committee of the Senate and the House of Commons under the very able joint chairmanship of two parliamentarians, and with the co-operation not only of many hon. members, but of many witnesses. This committee has prepared a remarkable report which has guided the government in drafting this measure. It has been very helpful to us in devising a solution.
I might also say that the press, members of the churches and the public at large have all been very helpful by their suggestions for reform. This proposed measure is not the sole product of one government, but rather the product of a social pressure which has been building up over the years to the point that this government had to seek a solution. We are now living in a social climate in which people are beginning to realize, perhaps for the first time in the history of this country, that we are not entitled to impose the concepts which belong to a sacred society upon a civil or profane society. The concepts of the civil society in which we live are pluralistic, and I think this parliament realizes that it would be a mistake for us to try to legislate into this society concepts which belong to a theological or sacred order. These are very important and sacred concepts no doubt, but they should not by themselves be considered as the sole guide for a government of a civil society.
Because of this it was necessary to find a remedy for these evils, and that is what this

December 5, 1967
Divorce Law Reform
government has attempted to do by this measure. The first point we tried to solve was the idea that even before dealing with divorce we must deal with the problem of strengthening the institution of marriage. This was brought home to us with great force and wisdom by many churchmen who appeared before us. They emphasized that the marriage is the important thing and that divorce is only a remedy to an unsatisfactory situation. We realize that marriage itself is the important aspect of any law which purports to deal with marriage and divorce. It is for that reason we wrote into this law at practically every stage provisions for reconciliation. This is true in respect of our definition of condonation, in respect of the obligations put upon lawyers who have clients asking for opinions in divorce matters, and in respect of the courts which hear petitions for divorce at the inception of the case, and even after the decree nisi has been granted. At all these stages we have written reconciliation concepts or procedures into the law.
This is a very important aspect of our law. Admittedly it is a concept which did not exist in this form in previous divorce laws in this country. We realize further that this whole situation requires more than just the adoption of a law. It requires that the government study on a continuing basis the effects of this law on marriage and study ways and means whereby reconciliation can be improved and bettered. This will mean that we will not only have to carry out research in respect of the consequences of this law and the way it operates, but we will have to continue to consult with provincial authorities, private organizations and churches. This was the first point we tried to deal with in this measure.
The second thing we tried to do was weed out the legal impediments to remarriage in cases where a previous marriage had broken down. As one hon. member pointed out last night, the consequences of our archaic divorce law is that many thousands of people-I think the figure of 500,000 was mentioned last night and the Canadian Bar Association also came up with some large figure-are involved in common law relationship in this country. This is a situation contrary to the desires of even those who believe most in preserving marriage.
These are people who cannot remarry because the present divorce laws do not create a situation in which they can get a divorce, or because they are too sincere to go through the sham proceedings so often

required to obtain a divorce under our present law. The remedy we envisage is first to preserve marriage and second to make better marriages possible by weeding out the legal impediments which now prevent remarriage and the formation of happy couples. This is because the bonds of former marriages have not been untied.
Although the idea of divorce is still repugnant to many people in this country-and I respect the reasons for which many people oppose the idea, as a matter of conscience, or religious or moral beliefs-when these reasons are applied to the legislative program of a country, it means imposing on a great majority the beliefs of perhaps a small minority.
[DOT] (8:50 p.m.)
As I said earlier, I think one of the fundamental tasks we must achieve in this parliament is to avoid mixing sacred and the profane. We must realize we are living in a pluralistic society, and even though some laws may be repugnant to the morals of individual members they must realize that we are all here to legislate not our own personal morals upon the country but to seek solutions to evils which arise in a civil society and which must be solved by civil or criminal laws.
I think this is what has guided us in our decision to reform these laws. This is a good opportunity for me to say that because of this I did not find it necessary to recommend that the vote on divorce laws be a free vote, in the sense that the expression is used in this house. I respect those hon. members who for moral reasons do not agree with the concept of divorce. I think those who believe that marriage is indissoluble, and it is a very worthy belief, are in the position of asking themselves nonetheless whether this law is necessary now to find a solution to a real social evil.
I think I have shown, and hon. members know from experience, that these evils arising from our unsatisfactory divorce laws are very present in this society. I should say, for the benefit of those people who have moral doubts, that this is merely a permissive law. It is a law that will permit the breaking of the marriage link but which obliges no one to remarry, if this is against his principles. This legislation is just dealing with the civil link; it is not dealing with moral beliefs. Indeed I think it is theologically acceptable, even to the most stringent of Christians, that if an annulment of marriage is obtained under
December 5, 1967



church laws, canon laws, and if the only way to dissolve the remaining civil link is through divorce, then divorce in such a case is perfectly admissible.
I think this is borne out by the very large support we have had from many of the Christian churches in Canada for the reform of the divorce laws. I want to thank particularly the authors of a brief which was presented to me by representatives of the Anglican Church of Canada, the Canadian Catholic Conference, the Lutheran Council in Canada, the Mennonite Central Committee, the Presbyterian Church in Canada and the United Church in Canada. They, to single out this example, brought forth a very interesting and well thought out brief. Indeed, in some aspects they have gone perhaps further in the area of grounds for divorce than this government has gone in the law that is before hon. members.
I will explain later why we have not felt it wise on legal grounds to go quite as far as the churches have recommended; but surely the fact that they were prepared to go further than us should reassure those members who feel that on grounds of conscience they should hesitate before voting for this law.
Having gone through the analysis of these evils, and seeing that the only proper remedy was to bring in a new divorce law, this is what we proceeded to do.
I should say at this point that we are not attempting in this law to deal with the causes of divorce. One hon. member last night, when speaking at the resolution stage, pointed out that it would be important to deal with problems of poverty, slum clearance, alcoholism and other such evils. This is quite true in a sense. The breakdown of marriage is not something that happens in a vacuum; it is something that is very often brought on by social conditions or evils with which this legislation does not attempt to deal. We are dealing only with the consequences of these social evils. I hope hon. members realize that in a divorce law we cannot do much more than this.
The government through its social legislation, and indeed the provincial governments through their various forms of legislation, have attempted to weed out all these evils in society, some of which lead to marriage breakdown. But I think it would be unnecessary in this law to try to deal with all these causes of divorce. We have to legislate on this particular subject, and I hope hon. members will not think it is because the government is not aware of these other causes of
Divorce Law Reform
divorce that it has not attempted to legislate on them.

Therefore, Mr. Speaker, since a legislation on divorce was to be drafted, I must say that the bill now before the house reflects our concern to respect the beliefs, the traditions and the customs of the various groups which make up our composite society.
This would seem obvious to anyone who would look at the provisions concerning the jurisdictions of courts, the rules governing procedure and proof. We did not want to disturb the administration of justice in the provinces by proposing new rules likely to confuse trial lawyers used to provincial regulations.
That is why, in principle, provincial superior courts of civil jurisdiction will now have jurisdiction in divorce matters.
There will be an exception, of course, in the case of Quebec and Newfoundland, but in our view,-and I feel I made that point quite clear last evening and, at the same time, it is a wish that I express-this exception for those two provinces is of a purely temporary nature. Moreover, as long as provincial laws of procedure do not come into conflict with the provisions of the present legislation, or with the rules of practice that competent courts may adopt, they will apply to divorce proceedings.
Finally, I wish to add that the laws of evidence in the province where divorce proceedings are started will apply to those proceedings.
At this point, Mr. Speaker, I should like to emphasize that in drafting this divorce legislation, we have taken into account the need to reconcile in the same act the procedures and concepts that belong to different statutes and mentalities.
For instance, when we decided that if divorce proceedings were to be taken let us say, in the province of Quebec, before the Court of the Exchequer, they would follow the provincial evidence act. We decided to include a section in the act authorizing the lawyers and parties taking proceedings in the province of Quebec to be governed by the provincial evidence acts.
Members will see that clause 20 of this bill is an innovation in this field, and I think it illustrates the real efforts we made to ensure in the drafting of the bill that we would bring a solution to a real social evil, while respecting provincial jurisdictions as

December 5, 1967

much as possible, all the evidence acts, all procedures and even the various ways of setting up courts in the different provinces.
So we have here the legislation that really represents my idea of a federal act, an act that applies to citizens ruled by provinces with quite different judicial systems. For this reason, Mr. Chairman, I took the liberty, a while ago, on the point of order, of noting that we had made all possible efforts so that all the citizens of this country, whatever their language affiliation, be treated equitably under this legislation.
The procedure before the courts is not the only indication of our concern over provincial differences. There is more. All provinces are not agreed on the measures to be taken to minimize the difficult consequences of a broken marriage, that is to say that in various provinces there are laws that vary from one province to another as far as alimony or the custody of children, for instance. That is why we have provided that during the divorce proceedings and in handing down the decree, the court dealing with the question of divorce-the very same court which is consequently in a position to know the circumstances and consider the parties-this court may order provisional or complementary measures appropriate to the parties and the children, taking into account all circumstances including the principles and customs recognized by the society in which they live.

speechtext:
I do not mind talking a little about this. It will disturb the argument of my speech but I cannot blame the hon. member for not finding it a very coherent sequence. There is no harm in giving a short explanation at this point, though I may have to deal with it at greater length during the committee stage.
In short, the reason is that when we are dealing with divorce we are dealing with certain fundamental rights possessed by citizens of this country. We are dealing with something much more fundamental than property rights or money matters. When we are dealing with the latter, we do have courts

at different levels which deal with various questions affecting property rights according to their importance.
I feel however that when we are dealing with marriage and divorce we should go to the superior courts, which in our society are traditionally called upon to decide upon the basic rights of human beings whether in civil or in criminal matters.
I realize that one of the reasons the joint committee wanted the county courts to exercise jurisdiction in this matter was because it wanted to make sure that the court would not be too removed from the people. My only comment on this is that the superior courts, or the supreme courts as they are called in some provinces, are not removed from the people. They all have district or circuit courts which go to the people, and on balance I felt it better to continue to use the higher courts, especially at the outset when we are breaking new ground and asking our judicial system to determine the operation of important laws, and to create a whole jurisprudence, a whole system of case law, which will govern these matters for many years to come.

To return to the subject I was speaking about earlier, I only wish to add a word or two. I ask the hon. members to realize that this measure does not abrogate the provincial laws; in other words, the laws concerning affiliation, for example, which exist in the various provincial jurisdictions, are not abrogated by our legislation on divorce. They continue to exist. We are merely trying to deal here with the question of divorce and the consequences immediately attending this breakdown of marriage. That is why, Mr. Speaker, we have provided for this three month period during which we want to consult with the provinces to make sure, in all good faith, that the present legislation can be applied without too much difficulty in all the provinces. That is why also, as I said earlier, we have sent to the attorneys general of all the provinces a copy of the present legislation, which we will be happy to discuss with them.
So much the more so that as I said last night, the matter of judicial separation is not dealt with in this bill. That creates, Mr. Speaker, a strange situation. In my opinion, according to the constitution-and this opinion is shared by many more eminent constitutionalists than myself-judicial separation comes under federal jurisdiction, so that
December 5, 1967

legislation now governing the provinces in that field could not be amended by the provinces because they have no jurisdiction in that field. So when we are called upon to pass a bill on divorce, which will not deal with judicial separation, that law will give grounds for divorce which will be broader than the grounds for judicial separation existing in several provinces. It will follow that it will be practically an encouragement to people to start divorce proceedings instead of separation proceedings, and I realize that anomaly perfectly. That is the phenomenon which made us include in a first draft of the bill provisions dealing with judicial separation which would have run parallel to the provisions dealing with divorce, and once again because I believe in co-operative federalism and because I believe that in such a field it is important that the central government should have consultations with the provinces, especially with those which already have in their statutes provisions dealing with judicial separation.
In the case of Quebec, this is even more important, because this province is now in the process of reshaping or reviewing its Civil Code and I know that very capable people are precisely working on the chapters concerning marriage, filiation and other related subjects. I think this will eventually lead to consultations between the provinces and the federal government, because of this anomaly: the Civil Code of the province of Quebec, since it was adopted before confederation in 1866, contains clauses and even whole chapters which do not come under provincial jurisdiction and which the province of Quebec itself cannot amend.
For this reason, the federal government, who is aware that the Civil Code is an important monument for French-speaking society, is not only willing, but anxious, to co-operate with the province of Quebec, inasmuch as it is necessary, so that this monument may be amended essentially by the provincial government, but partly also, as I explained a moment ago, by the federal government, so that the essential, special structure of such a monument as the Civil Code is not broken. I think that that is one aspect of the responsibilities of a federal government which, I will say it again, must rule over provinces governed by various judicial systems. Incidentally, I might say, Mr. Speaker, that this is one reason why it is also important for French-speaking people to have civil servants and politicians in Ottawa who can express their point of view. That is about all
Divorce Law Reform
I wanted to say about this matter, Mr. Chairman.
[DOT] (9:10 p.m.)

Just before closing, I thought I would touch briefly on one other aspect, that of marriage breakdown. I said a moment ago that we had been very thankful for the cooperation we have received from many of the church groups who have guided us in our ideas about reconciliation in the divorce laws. They have, in their briefs, recommended some provisions with respect to marriage breakdown which we have decided not to follow quite in the way they suggested. I think in fairness, before closing, I should give a word of explanation on this aspect. Very careful consideration has been given to the recommendations of those who advocated the adoption of an unqualified marriage breakdown approach to divorce in this country. If such an approach were adopted it would, in my judgment, entail the creation of special courts with specialized personnel to administer the divorce laws of this country. This is so because I think it is wholly unrealistic to impose upon the existing courts of law, and the judiciary, an inquisitional approach coupled with what would be, in effect, broad administrative discretion in dealing with the subject matter of divorce.
Courts of law and judicial tribunals are concerned-
-with legal rights and liabilities, which means rights and liabilities conferred or imposed by law; and "law" means statutes or long settled principles. These legal rights and liabilities are treated by a judicial tribunal as pre-existing; such a tribunaj professes merely to ascertain and give effect to them; it investigates the facts by hearing "evidence" (as tested by long settled rules), and it investigates the law by consulting precedents.
This quotation is from an article by Mr. D. M. Gordon in the Law Quarterly Review, 1934. I should just add by way of contrast that administrative tribunals, when they are defined by law, base their decisions and orders not on legal rights, not on liabilities but on policy and expediency. It is essentially because of this, Mr. Chairman, that we have not introduced the marriage breakdown principle in its most naked form. We have, as hon. members have seen, put the marriage breakdown principle in the law, but we have tried to guide the courts by indicating what the evidence of breakdown should be. If hon. members read the law very carefully, they will see that some of the sections are quite wide.

December 5, 1967
Divorce Law Reform
Another reason for doing this, apart from the spirit of the civil law as opposed to administrative law, is that in fairness we should say we wanted to avoid a situation in which some courts would decide that there was no breakdown no matter what evidence was put before them, and that reconciliation was always possible. Some of those who believe in the indissolubility of marriage might be inclined to judge in this way. We did not want a situation to develop where some courts would not be granting divorces in any and all cases. We wanted to put in our law a direction to the courts that they must grant a divorce when certain evidences of breakdown or of offences exist.
For all of these reasons, we have adopted this way of proceeding. There is not much more I think I should attempt to say at this stage. I thank hon. members for the way in which they received the law at the resolution stage, and for their courtesy in listening to me at this present stage. I can only add that as we get along with second reading, and eventually to the committee stage of the bill, I will be guided by every loyal effort of every member of this house to improve this law in such a way as to remedy a situation that has long needed remedying in this country.

But, of course, in the province of Quebec people will still, be free to choose a course of action under the legislation concerning separation from bed and board and of estate contained in the civil code or under the divorce legislation. They will have a choice to make and if they decide to act according to the provincial legislation other than under the civil code, they will be governed of course by the provisions of the civil code. If they decide to act under the federal legislation on divorce, they will be governed by these provisions.
If the hon. member studies those provisions, he will find that we have tried to draft them so as to avoid any conflict with provincial statutes. Of course, people will have to choose between divorce and legal separation.
Besides, jurisprudence enlightens us on another problem, and it is probably one of those the hon. member has in mind. What about the separation of estate?
Now, hon. members will realize that in this legislation, we have not implemented the recommendations of the joint committee of both houses which suggested that the federal legislation on divorce also deal with the matter of separate maintenance. It is precisely because we consider that question of separate maintenance comes essentially under provincial jurisdiction that we could not deal with it in the present legislation.
It is certain that some possessions, those which perhaps come from the marriage tie
December 5, 1967

itself, could be regulated under federal jurisdiction. But in practice, since it will be very difficult to distribute these possessions which are often worth little in comparison with the personal property of the husband and wife, it would have been a mistake to try to decide how property should be divided by the present legislation.
I think that the jurisprudence of the Superior Court of the province of Quebec will continue to be applied, and that a divorce will automatically mean separate maintenance.
